questions.q: A student scores $82$ on an exam where the class mean is $74$ and the standard deviation is $5$. What is the student's standardized $z$-score?
What does a $z$-score of $-2.4$ indicate about an observation?
choices: The observation is $2.4$ standard deviations below the mean
The observation is $2.4$ units below the mean
The observation is in the 2.4th percentile
The probability of the observation is negative
questions.answer: A $z$-score measures the signed number of standard deviations an observation falls relative to the arithmetic mean; negative indicates below the mean.

questions.q: On Test 1, Alice scored $88$ (mean $80$, SD $4$). On Test 2, she scored $92$ (mean $85$, SD $5$). On which test did she perform relatively better compared to peers?
choices: Test 2 because her raw score was $92$ vs $88$
questions.answer: Test 1: $z_1 = \frac{88 - 80}{4} = 2.0$. Test 2: $z_2 = \frac{92 - 85}{5} = 1.4$. Performance relative to peers is higher on Test 1.

sections.heading: Section 2: Linear Transformations - Adding a Constant

questions.q: A dataset has mean $\mu = 50$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 8$. If $5$ points are added to every observation ($y = x + 5$), what are the new mean and standard deviation?
questions.answer: Adding a constant shifts all measures of center (mean increases by 5 to 55), but does not alter measures of spread (standard deviation remains 8).

questions.q: If a constant $c = 10$ is subtracted from every value in a dataset, which statistic changes?
questions.answer: Subtracting a constant shifts the center (median decreases by 10), but leaves all measures of spread (range, IQR, variance, standard deviation) unchanged.

questions.q: A teacher curves a test by adding 8 points to all student scores. How does this affect the shape of the score distribution?
choices: The shape remains exactly the same
The distribution becomes skewed to the right
questions.answer: Adding a constant is a rigid shift of the distribution along the axis; it has zero impact on the shape or spread.

sections.heading: Section 3: Linear Transformations - Multiplying by a Constant

questions.q: A dataset of temperatures in Celsius has mean $20^{\circ}\text{C}$ and standard deviation $4^{\circ}\text{C}$. Converting to Fahrenheit using $F = 1.8C + 32$, what are the new mean and standard deviation?
questions.answer: New mean: $1.8(20) + 32 = 36 + 32 = 68^{\circ}\text{F}$. New standard deviation: $|1.8| \times 4 = 7.2^{\circ}\text{F}$ (addition of $+32$ does not affect spread).

questions.q: If all observations in a dataset with variance $16$ are multiplied by $-3$, what is the new variance?
questions.answer: Multiplying by constant $b$ multiplies variance by $b^2$. Here $(-3)^2 \times 16 = 9 \times 16 = 144$.

questions.q: If every observation is multiplied by $0.5$, how does the IQR change?
questions.answer: Measures of spread are multiplied by $|b|$. With $b = 0.5$, the new IQR is $0.5 \times \text{old IQR}$.

questions.q: If an entire non-normal distribution with mean $\mu = 40$ and $\text{SD} = 6$ is converted to $z$-scores ($z = \frac{x - 40}{6}$), what are the mean and standard deviation of the standardized values?
questions.answer: Standardizing any distribution (regardless of shape) by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation always produces a new distribution with mean $0$ and standard deviation $1$.

questions.q: Does standardizing a skewed dataset into $z$-scores transform the distribution into a normal shape?
choices: No, standardizing changes center and scale but preserves the original skewed shape
Yes, standardizing always creates a standard normal bell curve
Only if the sample size is greater than 30
Yes, because the mean becomes 0 and standard deviation becomes 1
questions.answer: Standardization is a linear transformation ($z = \frac{1}{\sigma}x - \frac{\mu}{\sigma}$). Linear transformations never change the fundamental shape of a distribution.

questions.q: A runner's race time is at the 85th percentile of all competitors. What does this mean?
choices: The runner was faster than $85\%$ of competitors (finished with lower time than $15\%$ of competitors)
The runner scored an $85\%$ on the race
The runner finished in the top $85\%$
$85\%$ of competitors finished before this runner
questions.answer: In general percentile terminology, the $p$th percentile is the value such that $p$ percent of observations fall at or below it.
